extracted.intended_audience: writers, readers, and critics of poetry and prose (general educated literary audience)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating and producing 'wit' in literary writing: distinguishes true wit from false/contrived devices, gives tests, examples, and aesthetic principles for poets and prose-writers.

rubrics_metrics.name: True wit (resemblance/congruity of ideas)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every resemblance of ideas is not wit unless it be such an one that gives Delight and Surprise to the Reader; true wit generally consists in such a Resemblance and Congruity of Ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The likeness must not lie too near in the nature of things — obvious comparisons give no surprise and are not witty. Examples: a comparison that adds an unexpected quality (e.g. 'as white as snow' + 'as cold too') converts a plain similitude into wit. True wit underlies metaphors, allegories, parables, visions, and related devices; it aims to delight and to surprise rather than merely to ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: False wit (resemblance of words/letters/sounds)
rubrics_metrics.description: False wit chiefly consists in the resemblance and congruity of single letters (anagrams, chronograms, lipograms, acrosticks), of syllables (echos, doggerel rhymes), of words (puns, quibbles), or of whole sentences/poems cast into shapes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These devices are mechanical and superficial — they rest on verbal coincidences rather than on meaningful likenesses of ideas. They are criticized as being 'vox et præterea nihil' (a sound and nothing). Examples and anti-patterns are given throughout (anagrams, chronograms, acrosticks, shaped poems, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Punning: definition and linguistic test
rubrics_metrics.description: A pun is a conceit arising from the use of two words that agree in sound but differ in sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The practical test for a pun: translate it into a different language — if it vanishes under translation, it may be concluded to be a pun (i.e. only sound-based). Punning is therefore brittle: it often has no weight beyond the immediate sound-play. Historical note: rhetoricians have treated paragrams/puns as figures of speech, but they are distinct from 'true' wit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixed wit (part-word, part-idea) and its proper province
rubrics_metrics.description: Mixed wit consists partly in the resemblance of ideas and partly in the resemblance of words (a mixture of truth and falsehood).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mixt wit is more or less perfect depending on whether the resemblance lies more in the ideas or in the words. Its appropriate domain is the epigram or short occasional poems — prolonged use tends toward falsehood. Examples: Cowley, Waller, some Italian epic moments; Boileau rejects it. Treat mixed wit cautiously and prefer it in short forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delight and Surprise as essential properties of wit
rubrics_metrics.description: Delight and Surprise are essential to wit, particularly Surprise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A resemblance must both please and unexpectedly illuminate the reader; mere likeness without surprise is not wit. Craft comparisons and metaphors so they reveal something new rather than restate the obvious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propriety of words and thoughts adapted to the subject (Dryden)
rubrics_metrics.description: Wit (or good writing) as 'a propriety of words and thoughts adapted to the subject.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Addison notes this definition (Dryden) but also critiques it as too broad (it would extend to many kinds of correct writing, even Euclid). Use 'propriety' as a component of good writing but not a sufficient definition of wit on its own.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth/justness as the foundation of beautiful thought (Bouhours)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is impossible for any thought to be beautiful which is not just and has not its foundation in the nature of things; the basis of all wit is truth and good sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A thought must be grounded in reality or natural justice; cleverness without truth lacks value. Aim for thoughts that are 'just' and rooted in the nature of things, not merely fanciful verbal cleverness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural/classical simplicity over 'gothick' ornament
rubrics_metrics.description: A taste for the natural simplicity of the ancients is preferable; poets who lack strength of genius substitute extravagant foreign ornaments and contrivances ('Goths in Poetry').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer majestic simplicity and clarity derived from nature and strength of genius; avoid hunting after artificial ornaments or forced conceits to compensate for weakness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opposition (antithesis) as a source of wit
rubrics_metrics.description: Not only resemblance but opposition of ideas very often produces wit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use turns, antitheses, and contrasts to produce witty effects; this is another legitimate rhetorical route to surprise and insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience taste and reader-classes (Segrais)
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers differ in capacity: the lowest class ('les petits esprits') prefer the husk and rind of wit — quibbles, conceits, epigrams — while better readers value solid sense and elegant expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing, consider your intended audience: popular or lower-taste audiences may reward puns and epigrams, but lasting literary value aligns with judgment and truth. As readers improve, they typically abandon coarser tastes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanical contrivances and fashionable word-games as anti-patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific fashionable devices (anagrams, acrosticks, chronograms, lipograms, bouts-rimés, double rhymes, doggerel, shaped/altar poems, contrived echoes) are forms of 'false wit' and generally to be distrusted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay gives many concrete examples and historical anecdotes (e.g., chronograms on medals, bouts-rimés exercises, acrosticks circulated as political jests). These are pictured as time-consuming little tricks that require little capacity and produce ephemeral cleverness rather than substantial wit. Treat such devices as ornament at best and avoid letting them substitute for real thought.
